title: Consistency models, CAP and PACELC
summary: What a read may return once data has copies: linearizable to eventual on a timeline, the session guarantees users notice, and CAP and PACELC without the myths.

steps.title: Copies make reads interesting
body: As soon as data lives on more than one machine (replicas, caches, regions), a read can return an **older**
value than the latest write. A **consistency model** is the promise about which values a read may return.
```text
time ->        0 ms           50 ms            800 ms
primary   W(x=2) ok
Alice                   R(x) from replica -> 1   <- stale: she just wrote 2
| Model | A read returns... |
| **Linearizable** (strong) | the latest completed write, as if there were one copy and one clock |
| **Sequential** | some single order of all writes that every client agrees on, keeping each client's own order |
| **Causal** | anything a write depended on before the write itself (a reply never shows before its question) |
| **Read-your-writes** | at least your own latest write |
| **Monotonic reads** | never something older than what you already saw |
| **Eventual** | the latest value *eventually*, once writes stop; anything until then |
Stronger models cost latency (wait for copies) or availability (refuse when copies cannot be reached).
Most products need strong consistency for a few things and session guarantees for the rest.

steps.prompt: Match each model to its promise.
pairs: behaves like one copy: every read sees the latest completed write
a reply is never visible before the message it answers
you always see your own latest write
time never goes backwards for one reader
copies agree once writes stop, with no promise about when

prompt: **Symptom first.** Support tickets: "I post a comment, the page reloads, my comment is gone; it shows up a
few seconds later." Writes go to the primary; reads go to any replica. The dashboard shows:
options: A read-your-writes violation: the reload hits a lagging replica (replica-2 is 3 s behind) before it has the comment
The comment insert is failing and being retried
The cache TTL is too long
steps.explain: Async replicas lag. The author's next read must see their own write: route that user's reads to the primary for a short window after a write, or wait until the replica has replayed past the write's position (LSN).

steps.title: Giving users their session guarantees
body: You rarely need linearizability everywhere. You almost always need users to see **their own** changes, and
never to watch data go backwards. Common ways to get there with async replicas:
- **Stick to the primary after a write.** For N seconds (more than the usual lag) after a user writes, send
their reads to the primary. Simple; costs primary load.
- **Carry a position token.** After the write, return the primary's WAL position (PostgreSQL
`pg_current_wal_lsn()`). Before reading on a replica, check `pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()` is at least that far;
else wait a little or go to the primary.
- **Pin a session to one replica** for monotonic reads, so a reader never hops to a replica that is further behind.
- **Commit with `synchronous_commit = remote_apply`** on a synchronous standby, so reads there see the commit.
It makes every write wait for that standby.
- **Read-your-writes**: a session guarantee that a client always sees its own latest write, even when reads go to replicas.

steps.prompt: How strong does each operation need to be?
items: Selling the last seat on a flight
Electing the leader that holds a lock
A user editing their own profile and reloading
Showing a shopper their own cart
The like count on someone else's post
steps.explain: Uniqueness, the last unit of stock and locks break if two clients see different "latest" values. A user's own data needs read-your-writes. Counters other people glance at can lag.

steps.title: CAP and PACELC, honestly
body: **CAP** says: when a **network partition** happens (some nodes cannot talk to others), a replicated system must
choose for each request between **consistency** (refuse or wait, so nobody reads stale data) and
**availability** (answer from the side you can reach, possibly stale).
What CAP is **not**: a menu where you "pick two of three". Partitions are not optional; they happen. And with
no partition, CAP says nothing at all. "C" in CAP means linearizable, not the C in ACID.
**PACELC** fills the gap: if **P**artition, choose **A** or **C**; **E**lse (normal running), choose **L**atency
or **C**onsistency, because waiting for copies costs time on every request.
| System (as usually configured) | Partition | Else |
| Single primary with a synchronous standby (PostgreSQL, MySQL) | C: writes stop without the primary | C: every commit waits for the standby |
| Dynamo-style store at consistency ONE (Cassandra's cqlsh default) | A: any replica answers | L: one replica is enough |
| The same store at QUORUM | C (for the minority side) | C: wait for a majority |
| A globally replicated database with consensus per write | C | C: writes pay a cross-region round trip |
Most stores let you choose **per request**. Say which choice you made and why.

steps.prompt: Which statement about CAP is correct?
options: During a partition, each request either gets a possibly stale answer or no answer; with no partition, CAP does not constrain you
You can build a system that is consistent, available and partition tolerant if you buy good enough networks
A CA system is one that gives up partition tolerance, which is the usual choice for relational databases
CAP's C means the same as the C in ACID
steps.explain: Partitions are a fact, not a choice, so "CA" is not a real option for a distributed system. CAP only constrains behaviour during a partition, and its C is linearizability. PACELC adds the everyday latency trade-off.

steps.prompt: A write lands on the primary at t = 0. The replica applies it after 800 ms of lag. A read hits the replica at t = 300 ms. What does this print?
code: var seen = readAtMs >= lagMs ? string.Join(",", primary) : string.Join(",", replica);
steps.explain: 300 ms is before the replica caught up, so the read sees the replica's old state: no comment at all. That is eventual consistency, and exactly the support ticket from earlier.

steps.title: Check a session's guarantees
prompt: Given one user's session as events, find the first violation. `"W 5"` means the session wrote version 5;
- a read **older than the newest version this session wrote** breaks read-your-writes:
- else a read **older than the newest version this session has already read** breaks monotonic reads:
- otherwise `"ok"`. `<i>` is the 0-based index of the event. Read-your-writes wins when both are broken.
hints: Keep two numbers: the newest version this session wrote, and the newest it has read.
Check the read-your-writes rule before the monotonic rule, and only update the newest read after both pass.
template: Dojo.Eq("time goes backwards", "monotonic reads at 1", CheckSession(new[] { "R 7", "R 6" }));
Dojo.Eq("a later violation", "monotonic reads at 3", CheckSession(new[] { "R 3", "W 5", "R 6", "R 5" }));
Dojo.Eq("read-your-writes wins a tie", "read-your-writes at 2", CheckSession(new[] { "R 8", "W 9", "R 7" }));
Dojo.Eq("reading other people's newer data is fine", "ok", CheckSession(new[] { "W 2", "R 9", "W 3", "R 9" }));

steps.title: Build it: read replicas and lag
prompt: In the **System design board**, open *Read replicas and lag*. Reads that cannot be cached overload the
primary. Add read replicas to take them, and keep replica lag low enough that read-your-writes tricks stay
cheap. The board shows the exact goals.
steps.explain: Replicas scale reads, not writes, and every replica is a little behind. The lag you see on the board is the window in which a user could miss their own write.
